screens.title: Essential Material Design Widgets and User Interaction
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will build a practical understanding of Flutter’s Material Design widgets and how they let your app display information and respond to users. We’ll look closely at the fundamental content widgets — text, images, and icons — and then move to interaction widgets: the common button types, floating action button, and the text input field. You’ll learn how the TextEditingController and onChanged callback give you immediate access to user input, and why setState is necessary to refresh the UI when data changes. Along the way we’ll highlight common beginner mistakes like leaving onPressed null or forgetting to dispose controllers, so you can avoid subtle bugs and memory leaks. By the end you will be able to assemble a simple login layout and wire up controllers and callbacks to observe live updates. The practical skills here matter because almost every app needs readable content, responsive controls, and stable input handling. Think of this chapter as both a toolkit and a checklist: which widget to choose, how to style it, and how to keep your UI consistent and responsive under user interaction.

Essential Material Widgets

Learn which widgets to pick for displaying content and receiving input, how to wire callbacks, and how to update your UI safely. This knowledge unlocks predictable, accessible app behavior across screens.

In this lesson
Text, Image, Icon, Button families, FloatingActionButton, TextField with TextEditingController, onPressed/onChanged, and setState patterns.
Coming up
A hands-on starter login layout with two TextFields and an ElevatedButton; attention to controller lifecycle and common pitfalls.
Explore Key Topics
Practical widgets, event wiring, and safe state handling to keep UI and data in sync.
Visual Map
Display Widgets
Text, Image, Icon
Interaction
Buttons, FAB, Callbacks
Text Input
TextField, controllers, setState
Quick start
We’ll show code snippets and live-output style demos in a split view during the lesson to make wiring controllers and callbacks concrete.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on the concrete skills you’ll develop. First, you will identify and use the primary Material widgets for showing content: Text for styled strings, Image for bitmap content from assets or network, and Icon for vector glyphs. Practically, this means you can compose a readable app header, show a product photo responsibly, and decorate actions with meaningful icons. Second, you will implement button families — ElevatedButton, TextButton, OutlinedButton, and FloatingActionButton — and know when each is appropriate. You’ll learn the visual affordances that make an ElevatedButton feel primary and why an OutlinedButton is suited to secondary actions. Third, you will capture text input using TextField and manage that input with TextEditingController so you can read and programmatically set field contents. You will also see how onChanged gives low-latency reactions. Fourth, you will wire callbacks like onPressed and use setState inside a StatefulWidget to ensure the UI actually updates when data changes. Each objective pairs a practical demonstration — a login layout or a typed greeting — and a short verification task so you can check your competency.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Demonstrations

For interaction widgets, you’ll place three button variants and wire their onPressed callbacks to print messages to the debug console so you can confirm each button type behaves as expected and you can see the visual difference between primary and secondary actions. Each demonstration highlights a common pitfall to check for — such as null onPressed, missing dispose, or forgetting setState — and you’ll practice correcting those to reinforce the lesson.

screens.title: Text widget and TextStyle
screens.narratorSegment: The Text widget is the primary tool for rendering strings in Flutter and it is intentionally simple yet highly flexible. A Text widget accepts plain text and a style argument where you provide a TextStyle object to control fontSize, fontWeight, color, and family. Practically, this means you can create hierarchies like large bold titles, medium-weight subtitles, and small captions by adjusting style properties. For example, when you show an app header you might use a larger fontSize and a bold weight to establish visual hierarchy. A common beginner mistake is attempting to mutate a Text widget’s content directly rather than updating the underlying state; Text is rebuilt from state, so you should change the variable passed into Text and call setState if needed. Another important detail is accessibility: keep font sizes readable and contrast high so your text remains legible. Concrete example: build a greeting that updates when the user types their name into a TextField and you update a state variable. That strengthens your understanding of how Text reads from reactive state. Key takeaway: Text displays strings, TextStyle customizes appearance, and state drives dynamic updates.

content.html:
Core Concept

Text widget

Use Text with a TextStyle object to control fontSize, fontWeight, and color for readable hierarchy.

Definition & Notes
  • Text reads a string and displays it using the current theme by default.
  • TextStyle customizes appearance; combine with Theme.of(context).textTheme for consistency.
  • For dynamic text, change state and let Flutter rebuild the Text widget.
Key Takeaway

Keep style centralized via Theme and update only via state changes so Text reflects app data correctly.

Concrete example
Text(
  'Welcome to Cohortia App',
  style: TextStyle(
    fontSize: 28,
    fontWeight: FontWeight.bold,
    color: Colors.deepPurple,
  ),
)
Common misconception
Text is not a mutable surface. If the string changes, update the state variable and trigger a rebuild. Trying to 'change' a Text directly will not work.

screens.title: Image widget and loading strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Images add meaning and context to interfaces, but they come with performance and reliability concerns. Flutter’s Image widget supports multiple sources: Image. asset for packaged assets, Image. network for remote images, and Image. file or Image. memory for device files or raw bytes. When loading network images, it’s best practice to provide a placeholder and an error fallback so the UI remains stable even under poor network conditions. The fit property, such as BoxFit. cover or BoxFit. contain, controls how the image scales in its box and affects composition. A concrete pattern is to use Image. network with a loadingBuilder that shows a CircularProgressIndicator while bytes load, and an errorBuilder to display an Icon if loading fails. This keeps the layout predictable, avoids jarring jumps, and improves perceived performance. A common oversight is not constraining image dimensions, which can cause layout shifts or excessive memory use. Key takeaway: choose the correct source, show a placeholder for network images, and set fit and size constraints to maintain consistent layout. Image widget and loading strategies means prefer constrained sizes, placeholders for network images, and appropriate fit values to avoid layout shifts and provide graceful failure states.. In practical terms, displaying asset, network, and file images with graceful loading. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition

Image widget

Use Image.asset, Image.network, Image.file, or Image.memory depending on where the image comes from. Always plan for loading and errors.

Why placeholders matter
Showing a loading indicator or a static placeholder avoids sudden layout jumps when the remote image arrives and provides feedback that content is on its way.
Example code
Image.network(
  'https://via.placeholder.com/150',
  width: 150,
  height: 150,
  fit: BoxFit.cover,
  loadingBuilder: (context, child, loadingProgress) {
    if (loadingProgress == null) return child;
    return Center(child: CircularProgressIndicator(value: loadingProgress.expectedTotalBytes != null ? loadingProgress.cumulativeBytesLoaded / loadingProgress.expectedTotalBytes! : null));
  },
  errorBuilder: (context, error, stackTrace) => const Icon(Icons.error),
)
Checklist
  • Constrain width and height explicitly for predictable layout.
  • Choose BoxFit to preserve aspect ratio and composition.
  • Use loadingBuilder and errorBuilder for network images.
Key Takeaway

Plan for latency and failures; placeholders and explicit sizes keep the UI stable and performant.

screens.title: Icon widget and semantic meaning
screens.narratorSegment: Icons are compact symbols that communicate actions, status, or meaning at a glance. Flutter’s Icon widget typically draws from the built-in Icons class, giving you a large library of Material glyphs. Use icons to make actions discoverable: a heart for favorites, a trash for delete, or a plus for adding items. Keep in mind accessibility: always pair icons with text labels where the meaning could be ambiguous, and consider semantics for screen readers. You can control icon size and color to match the surrounding text and affordance. A frequent beginner error is relying on icon color alone to convey status; pair color with shape or text to ensure meaning for color-blind users. Icons are lightweight and inexpensive to render, but overusing them can clutter an interface. Key takeaway: choose clear, consistent icons and ensure each icon’s function is discoverable either through adjacent text or accessible labels. Icon widget and semantic meaning means pick clear icons and pair them with labels or semantics to avoid ambiguous actions and to support accessibility.. In practical terms, using vector icons to communicate affordances. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Core Concept

Icon widget

Use Icon(Icons.name) to draw vector glyphs. Tune size and color to match visual hierarchy and pair with labels for clarity.

Accessibility
If an icon performs an action, provide a textual label or semantic hint so assistive technologies can communicate its purpose.

Key Takeaway

Use icons for quick recognition but always make action meaning discoverable for every user.

screens.title: Buttons: Elevated, Text, and Outlined
screens.narratorSegment: Flutter provides several button families that express different levels of emphasis. ElevatedButton has a filled background and shadow to indicate a primary action — use it for the main positive action on a screen. TextButton is flat and minimal, suitable for less prominent actions or for inline links inside dialogs. OutlinedButton draws a thin stroke and no elevation; it works well for secondary actions that still need a visible affordance. All of these buttons share the onPressed callback; when onPressed is null the widget is disabled and painted in a muted style, which is why forgetting to assign onPressed is a very common beginner mistake. In practice, prefer ElevatedButton for commits like 'Save' or 'Login', use OutlinedButton for alternatives like 'Learn more', and TextButton for subtle dismiss or link-like actions. A concrete example: place an ElevatedButton labeled 'Submit', an OutlinedButton labeled 'Learn More', and a TextButton labeled 'Cancel' in the same row to establish visual priority. Key takeaway: choose the button by its emphasis and ensure onPressed is non-null when you expect interaction. Buttons: Elevated, Text, and Outlined means elevated = primary; outlined = secondary; text = subtle. always wire a non-null onpressed to enable the button.. In practical terms, when to use each button family and how their affordances differ. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pick by emphasis
keyIdea.text: Elevated = primary; Outlined = secondary; Text = subtle. Always wire a non-null onPressed to enable the button.

content.html:
Comparison

Button families

Understand visual prominence and pick the family that matches your action’s importance.
ElevatedButton — Primary
Filled and elevated; use for primary commit actions like Save or Login.
OutlinedButton — Secondary
Thin border, no elevation; good for secondary or alternative actions.
TextButton — Subtle
Flat, minimal; ideal for low-emphasis actions or inline links.
Concrete example
ElevatedButton(
  onPressed: () { print('Elevated Button Pressed!'); },
  child: const Text('Submit'),
),
TextButton(
  onPressed: () { print('Text Button Pressed!'); },
  child: const Text('Cancel'),
),
OutlinedButton(
  onPressed: () { print('Outlined Button Pressed!'); },
  child: const Text('Learn More'),
),
Common mistake
Leaving onPressed null disables the button. If you want an enabled-looking action, pass an empty closure rather than null when appropriate.

screens.title: FloatingActionButton (FAB)
screens.narratorSegment: The FloatingActionButton is a circular, elevated button used to represent the primary action on a screen — often an add, compose, or create action. Typically placed via the Scaffold. floatingActionButton slot, the FAB draws attention with its floating elevation and circular shape. Use a single FAB per screen to avoid ambiguity about the primary action. The FAB’s content is usually an Icon to summarize the action, for example a plus icon for add. When designing for accessibility and discoverability, provide a tooltip or content description, and avoid relying on icon-only affordances when the action may be unclear. Also consider placement: the FAB should not obscure important content; constrain layout so it floats over safe space or adjust padding. A common beginner misstep is using multiple FABs or using it for minor actions that don’t deserve primary emphasis. Key takeaway: reserve FAB for the most important, frequent action on a screen and pair it with a clear icon and tooltip. FloatingActionButton (FAB) means fab is for a single, prominent action per screen; pair with icon and tooltip and avoid multiple fabs that confuse users.. In practical terms, primary-screen action that floats above content. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition

FloatingActionButton

A circular elevated button representing the main action on a screen. Place with Scaffold.floatingActionButton and provide a tooltip for accessibility.

Design tips
  • Use one FAB per screen for a single primary action.
  • Choose a clear icon and provide a tooltip or semantics for clarity.
  • Ensure FAB doesn't obstruct important content — adjust padding or docking if necessary.
Visual example
+
Add item
Single, prominent create action — labeled via tooltip at runtime.
Key Takeaway

FABs draw attention. Reserve them for the primary, frequent action to avoid confusing users.

screens.title: TextField and TextEditingController
screens.narratorSegment: TextField is the primary widget for capturing typed input. To programmatically read or set the field’s content and to listen for changes, attach a TextEditingController. The common pattern is to create the controller in the State object, add a listener that updates a state variable, and dispose of the controller in the dispose method to avoid memory leaks. The decoration property accepts an InputDecoration to display hintText, labelText, prefix or suffix icons, and border styles. Use onChanged for low-latency reactions such as live validation, and use the controller when you need to read the full value or set it programmatically. A concrete example is a greeting that updates while the user types: the controller’s listener sets a _displayText variable and calls setState so a Text widget shows Hello, plus the typed name. A common mistake is omitting controller. dispose() in dispose; that causes lingering listeners and potential memory leaks. Key takeaway: controllers provide control and listeners provide immediate updates, but always dispose them when the State is removed. TextField and TextEditingController means use a controller to manage field content and dispose it in dispose() to prevent memory leaks; use listeners or onchanged to update ui live.. In practical terms, capture user text input and react to changes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Controllers + dispose

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

TextField with controller

class MyTextInput extends StatefulWidget {
  const MyTextInput({Key? key}) : super(key: key);

  @override
  State createState() => _MyTextInputState();
}

class _MyTextInputState extends State {
  final TextEditingController _textController = TextEditingController();
  String _displayText = '';

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    _textController.addListener(_updateDisplayText);
  }

  void _updateDisplayText() {
    setState(() {
      _displayText = _textController.text;
    });
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _textController.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Column(
      children: [ /* TextField and Text display */ ],
    );
  }
}
Explanation and tips
  • Initialize controller in State so you can call addListener and dispose later.
  • Prefer controller for programmatic reads and setState for UI updates.
  • Use InputDecoration to provide labelText and hintText that animate when focused.
Common Mistake

Not disposing controllers leads to memory leaks; always call controller.dispose() in dispose().

screens.title: Event handling: onPressed and onChanged
screens.narratorSegment: Callbacks are the mechanism through which widgets tell your app that the user performed an action. For buttons the onPressed callback is called when the user taps; for TextField onChanged is called as the text changes. These are simple function slots you provide, and the body of those functions executes your app logic. Always remember that onPressed set to null disables the button and removes interactivity. Use onChanged for immediate reactions like validation or suggestions, and use controller listeners for centralized handling when you need to read the full field state. When callbacks mutate state variables, wrap those changes in setState so Flutter knows to rebuild the widget tree and reflect the new values. A common misconception is that assigning a value to a variable will automatically update the UI; without setState the framework will not schedule a rebuild. Another practical pattern is to keep UI logic minimal inside callbacks and route heavier work to functions or to other services, keeping callbacks concise and testable. Key takeaway: callbacks are how user interaction reaches your app; keep them small, call setState for UI changes, and avoid long-running work directly on the callback thread.

Process Flow

Event handling

  1. User interacts with a widget (tap or type).
  2. Widget invokes its callback (onPressed, onChanged).
  3. Your callback updates state or triggers logic.
  4. If state changed, call setState to rebuild and reflect the update.
Pro tip
Keep callbacks small. For heavier tasks, call a separate async function and present loading state to the user.
Concrete examples
ElevatedButton(
  onPressed: () {
    // update state and call setState if necessary
    print('Elevated Button Pressed!');
  },
  child: const Text('Submit'),
),

TextField(
  onChanged: (value) {
    // live validation or update
    print('Text field value: $value');
  },
),
Common misconception: Changing a variable without setState will not update UI. Always call setState when the change should be visible.

screens.title: StatefulWidget and setState
screens.narratorSegment: StatefulWidget is the pattern you use when a widget needs to hold mutable state that changes over time. Pair it with a State object which stores state variables and lifecycle hooks like initState and dispose. When you change a state variable and want the UI to reflect that change, call setState with a function that mutates the state. setState schedules a rebuild for that State object so Flutter reconstructs the widget subtree under it using the new values. This model is efficient and predictable when used correctly, but beginners sometimes overuse setState at top-level widgets causing unnecessary rebuilds; prefer to keep state localized to the smallest widget that needs it. Another important practice is to perform disposal of controllers or streams in the dispose method to avoid resource leaks. For example, when a TextEditingController listener updates a display variable, the listener calls setState so the displayed greeting updates instantly. Key takeaway: setState is the explicit signal that tells Flutter to repaint with updated data, and structured state boundaries keep rebuilds minimal and efficient. Core Concept

StatefulWidget lifecycle

Practical pattern
Keep state as local as possible. If only a small widget depends on a value, make that widget stateful instead of its entire parent to reduce rebuild work.
Key Takeaway

Call setState when state changes and always dispose controllers. Localize state to avoid expensive rebuilds.

screens.title: Common mistakes and debugging tips
screens.narratorSegment: As you use Material widgets you'll encounter a few frequent issues. First, a button appears visible but does nothing: check whether onPressed is null. When null, Flutter intentionally disables the control. Fix: provide a non-null closure. Second, TextEditingControllers not disposed cause memory leaks: always call dispose in the State. dispose method. Tools like the Flutter inspector or analyzer warnings can help detect unused controllers. Third, UI not updating after changing a variable is often because setState was not called; remember that changing a plain variable does not cause Flutter to rebuild. Use setState around mutations for immediate visual updates. Fourth, network images causing layout jumps: constrain width/height and present a loadingBuilder placeholder to avoid jarring layout changes. For debugging, add print statements in callbacks to confirm execution, and use the devtools to inspect widget rebuilds. Key takeaway: many runtime issues come down to lifecycle and wiring; use small checks — onPressed, dispose, setState, and constraints — to find the root cause quickly. Warning

Common mistakes

  • Disabled buttons: onPressed is null.
  • Memory leaks: controllers not disposed in dispose().
  • Stale UI: changed variable without setState.
  • Layout shifts: unconstrained network images without placeholders.

  2. Dispose controllers in dispose to prevent leaks.
  3. Wrap state changes in setState to update UI.
  4. Use loadingBuilder and errorBuilder for network images.

Use small reproducible examples when debugging: isolate the widget and add prints to callbacks to confirm control flow.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will build a practical understanding of Flutter’s Material Design widgets and how they let your app display information and respond to users. We’ll look closely at the fundamental content widgets — text, images, and icons — and then move to interaction widgets: the common button types, floating action button, and the text input field. You’ll learn how the TextEditingController and onChanged callback give you immediate access to user input, and why setState is necessary to refresh the UI when data changes. Along the way we’ll highlight common beginner mistakes like leaving onPressed null or forgetting to dispose controllers, so you can avoid subtle bugs and memory leaks. By the end you will be able to assemble a simple login layout and wire up controllers and callbacks to observe live updates. The practical skills here matter because almost every app needs readable content, responsive controls, and stable input handling. Think of this chapter as both a toolkit and a checklist: which widget to choose, how to style it, and how to keep your UI consistent and responsive under user interaction.

These objectives focus on the concrete skills you’ll develop. First, you will identify and use the primary Material widgets for showing content: Text for styled strings, Image for bitmap content from assets or network, and Icon for vector glyphs. Practically, this means you can compose a readable app header, show a product photo responsibly, and decorate actions with meaningful icons. Second, you will implement button families — ElevatedButton, TextButton, OutlinedButton, and FloatingActionButton — and know when each is appropriate. You’ll learn the visual affordances that make an ElevatedButton feel primary and why an OutlinedButton is suited to secondary actions. Third, you will capture text input using TextField and manage that input with TextEditingController so you can read and programmatically set field contents. You will also see how onChanged gives low-latency reactions. Fourth, you will wire callbacks like onPressed and use setState inside a StatefulWidget to ensure the UI actually updates when data changes. Each objective pairs a practical demonstration — a login layout or a typed greeting — and a short verification task so you can check your competency.

On this page we translate objectives into demonstrable tasks you’ll perform. For displaying content, you’ll style a header using the Text widget and TextStyle to set size, weight, and color, and you’ll load an Image. network with a simple loading indicator to handle latency. That ensures you can present readable and resilient imagery. For interaction widgets, you’ll place three button variants and wire their onPressed callbacks to print messages to the debug console so you can confirm each button type behaves as expected and you can see the visual difference between primary and secondary actions. For text input, you’ll create a TextField linked to a TextEditingController and show typed text in a separate Text widget so you can verify both controller reads and live updates via onChanged. Finally, for state updates, you’ll use setState inside a StatefulWidget to rebuild when the controller’s listener updates a display variable. Each demonstration highlights a common pitfall to check for — such as null onPressed, missing dispose, or forgetting setState — and you’ll practice correcting those to reinforce the lesson.

The Text widget is the primary tool for rendering strings in Flutter and it is intentionally simple yet highly flexible. A Text widget accepts plain text and a style argument where you provide a TextStyle object to control fontSize, fontWeight, color, and family. Practically, this means you can create hierarchies like large bold titles, medium-weight subtitles, and small captions by adjusting style properties. For example, when you show an app header you might use a larger fontSize and a bold weight to establish visual hierarchy. A common beginner mistake is attempting to mutate a Text widget’s content directly rather than updating the underlying state; Text is rebuilt from state, so you should change the variable passed into Text and call setState if needed. Another important detail is accessibility: keep font sizes readable and contrast high so your text remains legible. Concrete example: build a greeting that updates when the user types their name into a TextField and you update a state variable. That strengthens your understanding of how Text reads from reactive state. Key takeaway: Text displays strings, TextStyle customizes appearance, and state drives dynamic updates.

Images add meaning and context to interfaces, but they come with performance and reliability concerns. Flutter’s Image widget supports multiple sources: Image. asset for packaged assets, Image. network for remote images, and Image. file or Image. memory for device files or raw bytes. When loading network images, it’s best practice to provide a placeholder and an error fallback so the UI remains stable even under poor network conditions. The fit property, such as BoxFit. cover or BoxFit. contain, controls how the image scales in its box and affects composition. A concrete pattern is to use Image. network with a loadingBuilder that shows a CircularProgressIndicator while bytes load, and an errorBuilder to display an Icon if loading fails. This keeps the layout predictable, avoids jarring jumps, and improves perceived performance. A common oversight is not constraining image dimensions, which can cause layout shifts or excessive memory use. Key takeaway: choose the correct source, show a placeholder for network images, and set fit and size constraints to maintain consistent layout. Image widget and loading strategies means prefer constrained sizes, placeholders for network images, and appropriate fit values to avoid layout shifts and provide graceful failure states.. In practical terms, displaying asset, network, and file images with graceful loading. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Icons are compact symbols that communicate actions, status, or meaning at a glance. Flutter’s Icon widget typically draws from the built-in Icons class, giving you a large library of Material glyphs. Use icons to make actions discoverable: a heart for favorites, a trash for delete, or a plus for adding items. Keep in mind accessibility: always pair icons with text labels where the meaning could be ambiguous, and consider semantics for screen readers. You can control icon size and color to match the surrounding text and affordance. A frequent beginner error is relying on icon color alone to convey status; pair color with shape or text to ensure meaning for color-blind users. Icons are lightweight and inexpensive to render, but overusing them can clutter an interface. Key takeaway: choose clear, consistent icons and ensure each icon’s function is discoverable either through adjacent text or accessible labels. Icon widget and semantic meaning means pick clear icons and pair them with labels or semantics to avoid ambiguous actions and to support accessibility.. In practical terms, using vector icons to communicate affordances. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Flutter provides several button families that express different levels of emphasis. ElevatedButton has a filled background and shadow to indicate a primary action — use it for the main positive action on a screen. TextButton is flat and minimal, suitable for less prominent actions or for inline links inside dialogs. OutlinedButton draws a thin stroke and no elevation; it works well for secondary actions that still need a visible affordance. All of these buttons share the onPressed callback; when onPressed is null the widget is disabled and painted in a muted style, which is why forgetting to assign onPressed is a very common beginner mistake. In practice, prefer ElevatedButton for commits like 'Save' or 'Login', use OutlinedButton for alternatives like 'Learn more', and TextButton for subtle dismiss or link-like actions. A concrete example: place an ElevatedButton labeled 'Submit', an OutlinedButton labeled 'Learn More', and a TextButton labeled 'Cancel' in the same row to establish visual priority. Key takeaway: choose the button by its emphasis and ensure onPressed is non-null when you expect interaction. Buttons: Elevated, Text, and Outlined means elevated = primary; outlined = secondary; text = subtle. always wire a non-null onpressed to enable the button.. In practical terms, when to use each button family and how their affordances differ. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The FloatingActionButton is a circular, elevated button used to represent the primary action on a screen — often an add, compose, or create action. Typically placed via the Scaffold. floatingActionButton slot, the FAB draws attention with its floating elevation and circular shape. Use a single FAB per screen to avoid ambiguity about the primary action. The FAB’s content is usually an Icon to summarize the action, for example a plus icon for add. When designing for accessibility and discoverability, provide a tooltip or content description, and avoid relying on icon-only affordances when the action may be unclear. Also consider placement: the FAB should not obscure important content; constrain layout so it floats over safe space or adjust padding. A common beginner misstep is using multiple FABs or using it for minor actions that don’t deserve primary emphasis. Key takeaway: reserve FAB for the most important, frequent action on a screen and pair it with a clear icon and tooltip. FloatingActionButton (FAB) means fab is for a single, prominent action per screen; pair with icon and tooltip and avoid multiple fabs that confuse users.. In practical terms, primary-screen action that floats above content. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

TextField is the primary widget for capturing typed input. To programmatically read or set the field’s content and to listen for changes, attach a TextEditingController. Callbacks are the mechanism through which widgets tell your app that the user performed an action.
